title: Point Cloud Processing for Robotics
definition: Point clouds are unordered sets of 3D points $\{(x_i, y_i, z_i)\}_{i=1}^{N}$ from depth sensors (LiDAR, RGB-D cameras). Processed by architectures like PointNet (per-point MLP + symmetric function for permutation invariance: $f(\{x_1, \ldots, x_n\}) = \gamma(\max_{i} h(x_i))$ where $h$ is a learned per-point function and $\gamma$ is a global MLP), PointNet++ (hierarchical grouping with farthest point sampling), or voxelization approaches.
intuition: A point cloud is like a 3D scan made of millions of dots. Unlike images (ordered grid), points have no fixed order — shuffling them should give the same result. PointNet's key trick: process each point independently, then take the max across all points to get a global summary. Like asking each witness for their observation, then taking the most extreme/notable one.
practical_example: Grasping pipeline: RGB-D camera $\rightarrow$ point cloud $\rightarrow$ PointNet++ segmentation $\rightarrow$ per-object point clusters $\rightarrow$ GraspNet grasp pose prediction $\rightarrow$ execution. Preprocessing: voxel downsampling ($0.005\,\text{m}$ voxel), RANSAC plane removal (table), statistical outlier removal. Typical scene: $\sim 10^5$ points after downsampling.
failure_mode: Sensor noise at object edges creates phantom points between objects. Transparent/reflective objects produce missing/incorrect depth. Symptoms: segmentation leaks between adjacent objects, grasps planned on phantom geometry. Fix: temporal point cloud filtering, use learned depth completion for specular surfaces, RGB-based segmentation as prior.
interview_answer: Point clouds are the standard 3D representation for manipulation. PointNet/PointNet++ handle the key challenge of permutation invariance through the symmetric function $f(\{x_1, \ldots, x_n\}) = \gamma(\max_i h(x_i))$. In practice, I preprocess with voxel downsampling, outlier removal, and workspace cropping. For manipulation, PointNet++ with per-point features works well for segmentation and grasp prediction. Key engineering detail: depth sensor choice matters — structured light (RealSense) has different noise characteristics than time-of-flight (Azure Kinect). For transparent objects, RGB-guided depth completion or multi-view fusion is necessary.

title: 6D Object Pose Estimation
definition: Estimating the full 6-DOF pose (3D rotation $R \in SO(3)$ + 3D translation $\mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^3$) of known objects from RGB or RGB-D images. The pose transforms a point from object frame to camera frame: $\mathbf{p}_{\text{cam}} = R\,\mathbf{p}_{\text{obj}} + \mathbf{t}$. Methods: template matching, keypoint detection + PnP, direct regression, render-and-compare. Rotation representations: quaternion $\mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{S}^3$, rotation matrix $R \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}$, 6D continuous representation (Zhou et al.).
intuition: Given an image of a mug on a table, figure out exactly where it is (translation: 30cm forward, 10cm left, 5cm above table) and how it's rotated (handle pointing right, tilted 15 degrees). This is the information a robot needs to plan a grasp. The hard part: rotation is tricky to represent — quaternions have double-cover ($\mathbf{q}$ and $-\mathbf{q}$ represent the same rotation), Euler angles have gimbal lock.
practical_example: FoundationPose: category-level 6D pose estimation using render-and-compare. Given a CAD model and an RGB-D observation, iteratively refine the pose by rendering the model at the current estimate and comparing to the observation. Loss combines mask IoU, depth $L_1$, and feature similarity. Works for unseen object instances within a category.
failure_mode: Symmetry ambiguity: a bowl looks the same from many angles, so multiple rotations are equally correct. Training with a single ground-truth rotation causes the network to average between valid poses. Symptoms: predicted rotation is incorrect but loss is low. Fix: use symmetry-aware loss functions (e.g., $\mathcal{L} = \min_{R_s \in \text{Sym}} d(R_{\text{pred}}, R_{\text{gt}} R_s)$), predict distributions over rotations, or use canonical orientation definitions.
interview_answer: 6D pose estimation maps visual observations to $SE(3)$ poses for robotic manipulation. Key design choices: the 6D continuous rotation representation (Zhou et al.) avoids discontinuities of quaternions/Euler angles. For known objects with CAD models, render-and-compare methods (MegaPose, FoundationPose) work well. For novel objects, category-level methods generalize across instances. The main challenges: symmetry (handle with symmetry-aware losses), occlusion (handle with multi-view fusion), and specular/transparent objects (handle with RGB-D fusion or specialized networks).

title: Object Segmentation for Manipulation
definition: Pixel-level identification of object instances in a scene. Instance segmentation assigns each pixel a label $y_i \in \{0, 1, \ldots, K\}$ where $K$ is the number of instances. Semantic segmentation labels each pixel by class. Panoptic segmentation combines both. For robotics: SAM (Segment Anything Model) provides zero-shot segmentation from prompts (points, boxes, or text).
intuition: Before a robot can pick something up, it needs to know which pixels in the image belong to which object. Segmentation draws those boundaries. SAM changed the game: instead of training a custom model for each object category, you can point at or draw a box around anything and get a high-quality mask.
practical_example: Tabletop manipulation pipeline: RGB image $\rightarrow$ SAM with grid point prompts $\rightarrow$ instance masks $\rightarrow$ depth map + mask $\rightarrow$ per-object point cloud $\rightarrow$ grasp planning. For cluttered scenes: use SAM's 'segment everything' mode, then filter by workspace bounds and minimum area ($> 500$ px).
failure_mode: Under-segmentation in clutter: touching objects merged into one segment. Over-segmentation: one object split into multiple segments (especially textured objects). Symptoms: robot attempts to grasp two objects as one, or grasps only part of an object. Fix: use RGB-D fusion for segmentation, fine-tune on domain-specific data, add post-processing heuristics (convexity, size bounds).
interview_answer: Object segmentation is the first step in most manipulation pipelines. SAM has largely solved the general segmentation problem — it produces high-quality masks from minimal prompts (point clicks, bounding boxes). For robotics, the workflow is: SAM for masks $\rightarrow$ combine with depth for 3D reasoning $\rightarrow$ per-object processing. Challenges remain in heavy clutter (touching objects), transparent objects, and real-time performance. For production, I'd fine-tune SAM or use FastSAM for speed, combined with tracking (SAM-Track) for temporal consistency.

title: Camera Calibration and Hand-Eye Calibration
definition: Intrinsic calibration: focal lengths $(f_x, f_y)$, principal point $(c_x, c_y)$, distortion coefficients $(k_1, k_2, p_1, p_2, k_3)$. The projection model maps 3D to pixel: $$\begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} f_x & 0 & c_x \\ 0 & f_y & c_y \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X/Z \\ Y/Z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ Extrinsic calibration: transformation $T \in SE(3)$ between camera frame and world/robot frame. Hand-eye calibration: $AX = XB$ problem to find the fixed transform $X$ between camera and robot end-effector (eye-in-hand) or camera and robot base (eye-to-hand).
intuition: Intrinsics tell the camera 'what does my image mean in 3D?' (how pixels map to rays). Extrinsics tell the robot 'where is the camera in my coordinate system?' Without accurate calibration, a robot pointing at pixel $(320, 240)$ might reach 2cm off — which is the difference between a successful grasp and a miss.
practical_example: Eye-in-hand calibration: mount checkerboard on table, move robot to 15-20 poses capturing the board from different angles. Solve $AX = XB$ where $A$ = robot pose changes, $B$ = camera pose changes (from checkerboard detection). Validate: command robot to touch known points, measure error. Target: $< 2\,\text{mm}$ reprojection error.
failure_mode: Insufficient pose diversity: all calibration poses from similar angles $\rightarrow$ poorly constrained rotation estimate. Symptoms: accurate in calibration region, large errors elsewhere. Also: thermal drift changes intrinsics over time, especially for cheap sensors. Fix: capture from diverse angles/distances, recalibrate after thermal stabilization, use online calibration refinement.
interview_answer: Camera calibration is foundational for any vision-based robot system. Intrinsic calibration (OpenCV's calibrateCamera) gives you the lens model. The critical piece for robotics is hand-eye calibration — relating the camera to the robot frame. For eye-in-hand: solve $AX = XB$ with diverse poses. For eye-to-hand: similar but the camera is fixed. Key practical details: use at least 15 diverse poses, verify with physical touch tests (not just reprojection error), and recalibrate when the setup changes. The biggest mistake I see: not accounting for the time delay between capturing the image and reading the robot pose.

title: Depth Estimation for Robotics
definition: Recovering per-pixel depth $d(u,v)$ from visual sensors. Three paradigms: (1) Stereo vision — triangulation from two cameras with baseline $b$: $d = \frac{f \cdot b}{\text{disparity}}$; (2) Structured light — project known IR pattern (e.g., RealSense D400), recover depth from pattern deformation; (3) Monocular depth estimation — learn $d = f_\theta(I)$ from a single RGB image using scale-invariant losses like $\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i (\log d_i - \log \hat{d}_i)^2 - \frac{\lambda}{n^2}\left(\sum_i \log d_i - \log \hat{d}_i\right)^2$. Recent foundation models (Depth Anything, ZoeDepth, MiDaS) produce high-quality metric or relative depth from a single image.
intuition: A robot needs to know how far away things are to interact with them. Stereo vision works like human eyes — two slightly offset views let you triangulate distance. Structured light cheats by projecting a known pattern and seeing how it warps on surfaces. Monocular depth is the hardest: estimating 3D from a single 2D image, relying on learned cues like perspective, occlusion, and texture gradients — the same cues humans use when closing one eye.
practical_example: Depth pipeline for tabletop manipulation: Intel RealSense D435 (structured light, $1280 \times 720$ at 30 fps, range $0.3$-$3\,\text{m}$) for primary depth. For transparent objects where structured light fails, run Depth Anything V2 on the RGB image to get monocular depth, then fuse: $d_{\text{fused}}(u,v) = w \cdot d_{\text{sensor}}(u,v) + (1-w) \cdot \alpha \cdot d_{\text{mono}}(u,v) + \beta$, where $\alpha, \beta$ are scale/shift alignment parameters and $w$ is a confidence weight from the sensor validity mask.
failure_mode: Structured light fails on: transparent objects (IR passes through), specular surfaces (IR reflects away), outdoor scenes (IR sunlight interference), thin objects (insufficient pattern coverage). Stereo fails on: textureless regions (no features to match), repetitive patterns (ambiguous matching). Monocular fails on: metric scale (inherent ambiguity without known reference), unusual viewpoints not in training data. Symptoms: holes in depth maps, flying pixels at edges. Fix: multi-modal fusion (structured light + monocular), temporal filtering, confidence-weighted depth completion.
interview_answer: Depth estimation is the bridge between 2D perception and 3D robot interaction. In practice, I use a layered approach: structured light sensors (RealSense) provide reliable metric depth for most surfaces. For failure cases (transparent, specular), I fuse with monocular depth estimation (Depth Anything V2) after scale-shift alignment. The key engineering decision is sensor selection: structured light for indoor manipulation ($0.3$-$3\,\text{m}$), stereo for longer range, time-of-flight for outdoor. Monocular models have gotten remarkably good but still lack metric scale without calibration — I use them as a complement to active sensors, not a replacement. For production systems, always monitor depth validity masks and have fallback behaviors for low-confidence regions.

title: Affordance Prediction for Manipulation
definition: Predicting what actions an object or scene region affords — i.e., the action possibilities given the geometry, semantics, and physics. Formalized as learning an affordance function $\mathcal{A}: \mathcal{O} \times \mathcal{S} \rightarrow [0,1]^{H \times W}$ that maps an observation $o$ and a skill descriptor $s$ to a spatial affordance heatmap indicating where and how to interact. Can also predict dense affordance representations: for each pixel $(u,v)$, estimate the post-contact motion parameters $\{\hat{\mathbf{d}}, \hat{\theta}, \hat{p}_{\text{success}}\}$ (direction, rotation, success probability).
intuition: When you look at a mug, you instantly know: the handle affords grasping, the rim affords pouring from, the body affords pushing. Affordance prediction gives robots this same intuition — instead of recognizing 'this is a mug,' the robot sees 'this region is graspable, that region is pushable.' It shifts from object-centric to interaction-centric perception, which is what manipulation actually needs.
practical_example: Where2Act / AffCorrs pipeline: RGB-D observation $\rightarrow$ pre-trained visual encoder (DINOv2) $\rightarrow$ per-pixel feature extraction $\rightarrow$ affordance head predicts per-pixel action success probability for each primitive (push, pull, grasp, rotate). At test time: select pixel with highest $p_{\text{success}}$ for the desired primitive, extract local geometry to parameterize the action (approach direction from surface normal, gripper width from local curvature). Enables zero-shot transfer to novel objects via geometric/semantic similarity in feature space.
failure_mode: Affordance-action gap: the model correctly predicts that a region is graspable but the downstream controller fails to execute the grasp (e.g., approach angle not feasible due to clutter). Also: part-level ambiguity — a knife handle affords grasping, but the blade also has high 'grasp affordance' geometrically. Symptoms: robot attempts to grasp unsafe or infeasible regions. Fix: condition affordance prediction on robot reachability/kinematics, add semantic safety filters, train with contact-aware labels that include approach direction constraints.
interview_answer: Affordance prediction is a powerful paradigm shift from object recognition to interaction prediction. Instead of a detect-then-plan pipeline, affordances directly answer 'where can I interact and how?' The practical pattern: use a pre-trained visual backbone (DINOv2, CLIP) to extract per-pixel features, then train lightweight affordance heads for each manipulation primitive. This transfers remarkably well to novel objects because affordances correlate with local geometry and semantics, not object identity. Key insight: affordances should be conditioned on the robot's embodiment — what's graspable depends on the gripper. I combine dense affordance maps with kinematic feasibility checking to get actionable predictions.
